issues.legal_issue: An officer delegated the Board’s revisional powers may exercise the Board’s review power over an order made while exercising those delegated powers.
material_facts: The Commissioner had been delegated the Board’s revisional powers under the survey and settlement legislation.
The Board had a general statutory power to review its own orders, while the survey and settlement legislation contained no express review power for the Board.
The Commissioner’s predecessor made a revisional order, and the successor Commissioner purported to review it.
issues.conclusion: The Commissioner, when exercising the Board’s delegated revisional powers, could also exercise the Board’s review power over the resulting order.
issues.legal_principle: The Board could review its own orders under section 7 of the Orissa Board of Revenue Act, 1951, including orders made in its revisional jurisdiction under sections 6D, 15, 25 and 32 of the Orissa Survey and Settlement Act, 1958. Section 33 of the 1958 Act authorized delegation of the Board’s revisional powers. A delegate who personifies the principal may exercise the other powers attributable to the principal in relation to the delegated function; denying the delegate the ability to correct obvious errors would create an anomaly. The Court also relied on National Sewing Thread Co. Ltd. v. James Chadwick & Bros. Ltd.

predicates.delegate_exercises_principal_revision: An officer exercises revisional authority delegated to that officer by a principal authority.
predicates.principal_has_review_authority: The principal authority has power to review its own orders.
predicates.review_concerns_delegated_order: The review concerns an order the officer made while exercising the delegated revisional authority.

issues.definition: When an officer exercises a principal authority’s delegated revisional power and the principal has review authority, the officer may review an order made in that delegated proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: The principal authority cannot revise or review an order made by its delegate while the delegate acts as the principal authority.
material_facts: The Commissioner made the disputed order as the Board’s delegate, rather than exercising the Commissioner’s own independent authority.
The Board had not itself heard or decided the matter.
The question was whether the Board could revise or review the Commissioner’s delegated order.
issues.conclusion: The Commissioner’s delegated order was treated as an order of the Board and could not be revised by the Board; the Board also could not review it because the Board had not made the decision and review ordinarily belongs to the same decision-maker or that decision-maker’s successor.
issues.legal_principle: Under Roop Chand v. State of Punjab, an order made by an officer exercising delegated authority is treated as an order of the delegating authority and is not revisable by that authority as an order of an officer in the officer’s own right. Behari Kunj Sahakari Awas Samiti v. State of U.P. applied the same principle and held that such revision would amount to an impermissible indirect review. Review is distinct from appeal and should, in practicable cases, be heard by the same decision-maker or that decision-maker’s successor, as explained in Maharajah Maheshur Singh v. Government of India.

predicates.delegated_order_treated_as_principal_ord: An officer made an order while exercising delegated authority, so the order is treated as one made by the principal authority.
predicates.principal_seeks_to_revisit_its_own_unhea: The principal authority seeks to revise or review the order despite not having heard and decided the matter itself.

issues.definition: If a delegate’s order is treated as the principal’s order and the principal seeks to revisit a decision it did not hear, the principal cannot revise or review that delegate’s order.

issues.legal_issue: Review of an order made in revisional jurisdiction is confined to correcting mistakes or errors apparent on the face of the record and cannot become an appeal or a further revision.
material_facts: The Commissioner’s predecessor had made findings in a revisional order concerning title and possession.
The successor Commissioner reviewed that order and considered factual issues concerning title and possession.
A civil suit based on title was pending, and the Supreme Court left the merits of title and possession open for determination in that suit.
issues.conclusion: The review power was limited to correcting mistakes or errors apparent on the face of the record; the Court did not determine whether the Commissioner’s particular review order exceeded that limit.
issues.legal_principle: Although section 7 of the Orissa Board of Revenue Act, 1951 authorized the Board to review its orders and pass such orders as it thought fit, review of an order made in revisional jurisdiction is narrower than appellate or revisional jurisdiction. The Court held that the review power was intended to correct mistakes or errors apparent on the face of the record, consistently with rule 43 under the 1958 Act, and disagreed in part with Ramakanta alias Ramesh Chandra Jagdebrai v. Gaji Pratap Singh insofar as that decision treated the review power as wider than Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.review_of_revisional_order: A reviewing authority is considering an order that was made in the exercise of revisional jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When the order under review was made in revisional jurisdiction, the review output is confined to correcting apparent errors.

issues.legal_issue: When a title-based civil suit is pending and appellate consideration of the merits could prejudice the parties, the title and possession questions may be left for decision in that suit.
material_facts: The State had filed a pending civil suit based on title, not merely to set aside record-of-rights entries.
The parties disputed title and possession of the land.
The Supreme Court considered that expressing views on the merits could seriously prejudice either side in the pending suit.
issues.conclusion: The Court left the findings and observations in the administrative orders open and directed that the civil court decide the title and possession questions according to law and the evidence, uninfluenced by the relevant appellate and administrative observations.
issues.legal_principle: A pending title-based civil suit that is not barred by section 29(2) of the Orissa Survey and Settlement Act, 1958 remains available to determine title and possession. To avoid prejudicing that determination, the Court left the merits open for decision by the civil court on the evidence produced by the parties.

predicates.pending_title_suit: A civil suit based on title is pending and includes disputed questions of title or possession.
predicates.appellate_merits_risk_prejudice: The appellate court’s consideration of the merits could prejudice a party’s case in the pending suit.

issues.definition: If a title suit is pending and appellate consideration of the merits could prejudice it, the title and possession questions are left for the civil court.

issues.legal_issue: While a civil suit concerning land with tree and forest growth is pending, the parties may be directed to maintain the existing condition and refrain from removing that growth or its produce.
material_facts: The pending civil suit concerned land containing tree and forest growth.
The dispute concerned the parties’ rights in the land and its forest growth.
The Court directed both parties to preserve the existing condition of the land and not to cut trees or remove forest produce pending disposal of the suit.
issues.conclusion: Both parties were directed to maintain the status quo on the land and not to interfere with the tree and forest growth, including by cutting trees or removing forest produce, while the suit remained pending.
issues.legal_principle: The Court imposed interim protective directions to preserve the disputed land and its forest growth pending resolution of the title suit; it also directed that there be no transport of the forest produce during that period.

predicates.pending_land_suit: A civil suit concerning the parties’ rights in land is pending.
predicates.disputed_land_has_forest_growth: The land in dispute contains trees or forest growth.

issues.definition: When a land suit is pending and the disputed land has forest growth, the parties must preserve the land and that growth.
